title: Chapter 185: Is Your Brain Filled with Lead?
html:
“Get in, and don’t try anything funny.”

Clutching the rooster and the cat, Chen Ge climbed into the police car. The officer’s tone suggested that this time, matters might have become rather serious.

“Thank God, you’re okay.” There was another person sitting in the backseat. His face was tense, but his voice was familiar.

“Liu Dao? What are you doing here? Did you call the police?” Strangely at ease in the patrol car, Chen Ge felt more sleepy than worried. “And why was the livestream suspended? What was our peak audience? My follower count jumped to 150,000.”

“How can you still care about the livestream?” Liu Dao seized his arm. “Brother, didn’t you say everyone in the hospital was an actor from your Haunted House? I vouched for you to the police, and you sent me straight to hell.”

“Some of my employees were in the hospital. You simply couldn’t see them.” Chen Ge felt no shame in saying it. He had brought the Pen Spirit, Xiaoxiao, and the white cat from the Haunted House for the broadcast.

“I’m not trying to blame you. It’s just…” Liu Dao’s expression collapsed. “Forget it. I should have taken more precautions. To be fair, you fooled plenty of viewers too.”

“What are you talking about? Mind explaining it to me.” Chen Ge wanted to pet the white cat’s head but was warned off by the cat’s cruel gaze.

Liu Dao threw up his hands. “If someone enters an abandoned mental hospital at midnight, finds victims locked in cages, and gets chased by axe-wielding murderers, shouldn’t he be afraid?”

“Yes, fear is the appropriate reaction.”

“The problem is that you chased those murderers through the building with a massive hammer for at least twenty minutes. Anyone watching would assume it was staged!” Liu Dao was close to breaking down. “I’ve worked in livestreaming for four years, and I never imagined a host would chase an actual murderer. Weren’t you afraid? Is your skull filled with lead?”

“You’re exaggerating. I only did what any law-abiding citizen should,” Chen Ge insisted. “I have a strong sense of justice. Seeing what the victims endured made me so angry that it overwhelmed my fear. That’s why I pursued the murderers.”

Chen Ge was loud, and the two policemen in front could hear him clearly.

“It’s too late for explanations. This is my fault; I should have called the police sooner.” Liu Dao massaged his temples. “Someone reported the stream soon after it began, but I assumed Qin Guang’s people were causing trouble and ignored it. When the audience reached 400,000, someone on my team demanded we contact the police, and I overruled them. Then the stream passed 600,000 viewers and broke the record for a new host. I finally felt something was wrong. You were shouting and swinging a cleaver at empty air, but I thought it was part of the performance. Out of sheer greed, I forced Sister Lee to keep broadcasting.

“Only when you entered that ward and the screen went black did I understand how serious it was and call the police.” Relief softened his voice. “What’s done is done. At least you’re safe.”

Liu Dao sighed, removed a small pill bottle from his shirt, and popped two pills into his mouth.

“What are those?”

“Angina medication. Leave me alone. This is my first time in a police car, and I need to calm down.”

At the city police station, Liu Dao and Chen Ge were taken to separate interview rooms. The officers questioned Chen Ge about every detail, and he maintained his earlier account: he had stumbled onto a criminal plot and fought back to protect the victims. The entire encounter had been broadcast, providing all the evidence he needed.

What troubled the police was that all the evidence identified Chen Ge as another victim—yet this particular “victim” had aggressively hunted the culprits.

After the interrogation, the police did not show any sign that they were going to let him go. “Mr. Chen, we need to have a meeting to discuss your situation.”

“All right, but can I have my phone? I’d like to tell my family I’m safe.” In truth, Chen Ge wanted to call Inspector Lee. This incident was different: the broadcast had not remained within a small niche. More than 600,000 people had watched it, and the situation had escaped anyone’s control.

“Please wait patiently.” The police officer rejected Chen Ge’s request and left the interrogation room. It was not until noon that the door opened again. Chen Ge, who had been fully cooperative, turned to look at the door.

A slightly heavyset officer stood in the doorway, wearing a uniform different from the others.

“Captain Yan?” Chen Ge was surprised. This was the officer who had presented his commendation after the Ping An Apartments case.

“Come with me. Someone wants to meet you.” Unlike during their last meeting, Captain Yan looked grave. Chen Ge rose slowly, wondering, Am I about to meet someone important?

They walked down the corridor and stopped outside another room. Through its glass panel, Chen Ge saw that the girl from the cage was safe. Wrapped in a police jacket, she cowered in a corner and clutched a bottle of water. She trembled incessantly, refused to speak to anyone, and did not even dare sit in the chair.

A middle-aged man stood nearby. Chen Ge had never seen anyone break down so completely. The man appeared to be her father. He called her name over and over, but she remained unresponsive, still imprisoned by terror.

“Go in, the father wants to meet you.”

The moment Chen Ge entered, the father rushed toward him, too overcome with emotion to complete a sentence.

…

About ten minutes later, Captain Yan and Chen Ge left the room.

“We spent the morning determining whether your actions violated the law. Before the discussion ended, I brought those two here.” Captain Yan looked through the window. “Without you, the girl might have spent the rest of her life in a cage, while her father spent his searching for the only family he had left.”

Chen Ge struggled to contain his emotions. The girl was safe, but the wounds in her heart would take years to heal.

“You’ve done good this time.” Captain Yan turned to Chen Ge. “After our discussion, we decided to temporarily ban your livestream, but as compensation, we’ll award you a record of merit.”

Rather than punishment, temporarily suspending Chen Ge’s livestream was meant to protect him from people who might exploit his sudden popularity.

Chen Ge did not know what the record of merit entailed, but Captain Yan’s emphasis suggested it was valuable.

“Thank you, but I merely acted on my sense of justice. Sometimes I can’t help myself.” Chen Ge remained uncertain. His behavior last night had undeniably been reckless: armed with a cleaver and hammer, he had broken a suspect’s leg. “So am I truly free to go?”

“Don’t try to get information from me.” Captain Yan pointed at his uniform. “We will not cheer for violence, but never will we punish a good conscience and sense of justice.”
